title: Hebrews
subtitle: A priest forever, and a word to tired believers
lead: Hebrews is a sermon written down and sent with a letter's ending. Its author calls it 'this word of exhortation' (13:22) and never gives his name. It was written, in Greek that Origen already judged purer than Paul's and that scholars of Greek often rank the most polished in the New Testament, to a community of Christians who had once suffered bravely for their faith (10:32-34) and were now growing tired, skipping their meetings (10:25) and in danger of drifting away (2:1). Its answer to their weariness is not a list of rules but a vision of Jesus: the Son through whom God has spoken his last word, greater than the angels, greater than Moses, and above all a high priest.

No other New Testament book calls Jesus a priest by title. Hebrews reads the Greek Old Testament, especially Psalm 110:4 ('You are a priest forever, after the pattern of Melchizedek'), Jeremiah 31 and the Day of Atonement law of Leviticus 16, to show that Jesus has done once for all what the priests of the tent did year after year. Between the stretches of teaching come five warnings, some of the sternest in the Bible (6:4-6; 10:26-31), and then the great roll call of faith in chapter 11 and the call to run the race with eyes fixed on Jesus (12:1-2).
facts: Not named. Received as Paul's in the Greek East from early on (Clement of Alexandria; Origen, who thought the wording another's); long doubted in the Latin West. Barnabas, Luke, Clement of Rome, Apollos and Priscilla have also been proposed. Most scholars today think it was not Paul. See the authorship table.

Before about AD 96, when 1 Clement (usually dated about AD 96) echoes it. Many date it before AD 70, because it speaks of the tent's sacrifices as still being offered (8:4; 10:1-2); others place it between 70 and 90.
A Christian community under pressure, perhaps in or near Rome ('The people from Italy greet you', 13:24), perhaps mostly Jewish believers. See the audience.
A sermon ('word of exhortation', 13:22; the same phrase as a synagogue sermon in Acts 13:15) with a letter's closing greetings
Greek, which Origen already found purer than Paul's and which scholars of Greek often rank the most polished in the New Testament
better, Son, high priest, perfect, once for all, covenant, faith, Today
authorship: Nothing. The writer heard the gospel from those who heard the Lord (2:3), knows Timothy (13:23), and sends greetings from 'the people from Italy' (13:24). The title 'To the Hebrews' was added later.

Clement of Alexandria held that Paul wrote it in Hebrew for the Hebrews and that Luke translated it into Greek, which explains why its style resembles Acts (Eusebius, Church History 6.14). The oldest copy, the papyrus P46 (about AD 175-225), places Hebrews right after Romans among Paul's letters. Eusebius counted fourteen letters of Paul, while noting that some rejected Hebrews because the church of Rome disputed its authorship (3.3.5); Gaius of Rome counted only thirteen, and 'there are some among the Romans who do not consider this a work of the apostle' (6.20.3). Even in the late 300s Jerome wrote that it 'is not considered his, on account of its difference from the others in style and language' (Lives of Illustrious Men 5), and Augustine that 'most say' it is Paul's, 'though some deny this' (City of God 16.22).

Origen judged that 'the thoughts are those of the apostle, but the diction and phraseology are those of some one who remembered the apostolic teachings', and added: 'But who wrote the epistle, in truth, God knows.' He reported that some named Clement of Rome and others Luke (Eusebius, Church History 6.25.13-14).
Tertullian refers to 'an Epistle to the Hebrews under the name of Barnabas' (On Modesty 20). Barnabas was a Levite (Acts 4:36), which would fit the letter's interest in priesthood.

Martin Luther proposed Apollos, 'an Alexandrian by birth' and 'a learned speaker and strong in the Scriptures' (Acts 18:24). Luther's preface to Hebrews (1522) itself names no one: it calls the author 'an able and learned man, who was a disciple of the apostles' and says: 'Who wrote it is not known, and will not be known for a while; it makes no difference.'

Adolf von Harnack proposed in 1900 that Priscilla, with Aquila, wrote it, and that her name was dropped because she was a woman. In 11:32 ('Time will run out on me if I tell the story') the Greek word for 'I tell' is a masculine participle, which most take as against this view.

Most modern scholars doubt that Paul wrote it: the Greek is more polished than his, the style and method of argument differ, and the writer places himself among those who received the gospel second-hand (2:3), where Paul insists he received it from Christ (Galatians 1:11-12). Ancient opinion was divided: the Greek East largely received it as Paul's, with Origen allowing that the wording was another's, while the Latin West long doubted. No other candidate has won general agreement. The churches hold the letter as Scripture whoever wrote it, and the Plain English Translation follows the text as written.

audience.to: A community of Christians the writer knew well and hoped to visit soon (13:19, 23). They had heard the gospel from eyewitnesses, with signs and wonders (2:3-4). Some time before, they had endured public insults and persecution, stood by prisoners and accepted the seizure of their property (10:32-34), though they had not yet 'held out to the point of blood' (12:4). They knew the Greek Old Testament well. 'The people from Italy' send greetings (13:24), which may mean the writer was in Italy, or that Italians with him were greeting their home church, perhaps in Rome. If Rome, the earlier suffering may be the expulsion of Jews under Claudius, when Priscilla and Aquila 'had just come from Italy, since Claudius had given orders that all the Jews must leave Rome' (Acts 18:2); Suetonius writes that 'since the Jews constantly made disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus, he expelled them from Rome' (Claudius 25.4), an event most scholars date about AD 49-50.
audience.why: The readers were tired. Their hearing had grown sluggish (5:11); some were missing the meetings (10:25); they were tempted to throw away their confidence (10:35) and to drift back into a safer life. The writer answers by showing them how great their Lord is and how much they would lose: the Son is better than the angels, than Moses, than Aaron; his one sacrifice has opened the way into God's presence; and the faithful of old endured without seeing what the readers now have. Knowing the readers changes the reading: the warnings of chapters 6 and 10 are a pastor's alarm for people he loves ('about you, beloved, we are persuaded of better things', 6:9), and the comparisons with the temple and the law are meant to keep them from going back, not to attack Jews outside the church.
views: Jewish believers tempted back to the synagogue

Many hold that the readers were Jewish Christians, perhaps in Rome, tempted to return to Judaism, where they would be safe from the shame of following a crucified Messiah and could share again in the familiar priesthood, sacrifices and festivals. The title 'To the Hebrews', the heavy use of the law and the temple, and the warnings against going back fit this view.

Others note that the letter never mentions circumcision, Gentiles or the synagogue, and that Gentile converts also learned the Greek Old Testament. On this view the danger was weariness and fear of persecution, and the comparisons with the old covenant show the greatness of Christ rather than answering a pull toward Judaism.

A minority place the readers in Jerusalem or Palestine, close to the temple, or in Alexandria, Antioch or elsewhere. The greeting from 'the people from Italy' and the early use of Hebrews by 1 Clement in Rome lead most to favor Rome.

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads Hebrews as a sermon to a real community: who they were (Jewish or mixed, in Rome or elsewhere), what they had suffered, whether the temple still stood, and what pulled them away. Draws on Acts, Suetonius, 1 Clement and the letter's own hints.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the book was made: who wrote it, when, in what genre (a homily), with what structure, and from what background (Jewish apocalyptic, Philo's Platonism); how it uses the Greek Old Testament; and what its manuscripts read, from P46 on.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Follows the craft of Greek often ranked the most polished in the New Testament: the one-sentence prologue, the alternation of teaching and warning, chains of quotations, arguments from lesser to greater, key words such as 'better', 'perfect' and 'once for all', and the rhetoric of the roll call.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads Hebrews as the most Jewish argument in the New Testament: priesthood, sacrifice, covenant and the Day of Atonement, Melchizedek in Qumran, Philo and the rabbis, angels at Sinai, and the honest question Jewish readers ask about supersession.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Traces how the churches read Hebrews: the fathers' use of 1:3 against Arius, Chrysostom's homilies, the early Latin doubts, Luther's preface, Calvin's commentary, and the long debates over 6:4-6, priesthood and the sacrifice of the Mass.

sections.b:
Hebrews is best read aloud in one sitting, as a sermon. It moves in waves: a stretch of teaching about Christ, drawn from an Old Testament text, then a warning or an appeal that applies it ('So...', 'Let us...'). The teaching is about who Jesus is and what he has done; the appeals are about holding on. The appeals are the reason for the teaching: the writer wants tired believers to see how much they have in Christ and how much they would lose by drifting away.

The central claim is in 8:1: 'the high priest we have is of that kind'. Everything before leads up to it (the Son, faithful and merciful, called after the pattern of Melchizedek), and chapters 8-10 explain it (a better covenant, a better tent, a better sacrifice, once for all). Chapters 11-13 turn the teaching into endurance, faith and life together.

Scholars have long debated how Hebrews is put together, because it weaves teaching and warning so closely. Albert Vanhoye's study of its literary structure (1963) and George Guthrie's text-linguistic analysis (1994) are two influential attempts to map it. Most agree on the main movements: the Son greater than the angels (1-2), than Moses (3-4), and the high priest after the pattern of Melchizedek (4:14-10:18), followed by the call to faith and endurance (10:19-13:25).

The word 'better' (kreittōn) appears thirteen times in Hebrews, twice as often as in all the rest of the New Testament: a better name, better things, a better hope, a better covenant, better promises, better sacrifices, a better possession, a better country, a better resurrection, blood that speaks better than Abel's. The comparison is never between bad and good. Hebrews honors the angels, Moses, Aaron, the tent and the law as God's gifts; its claim is that what God has now given in his Son is better still, and final.

Hebrews says that God has spoken his final word in the Son, that the Levitical priesthood was not final, that a change of priesthood brings a change of law (7:12), and that the first covenant is 'old' and 'close to disappearing' (8:13).

Christians have long read such lines as saying that the church has replaced Israel. Justin Martyr, in the 100s, told a Jewish partner in debate that 'the true spiritual Israel... are we who have been led to God through this crucified Christ' (Dialogue with Trypho 11), and later readers used Hebrews to justify contempt for Jews. In 1965 the Second Vatican Council, while still calling the church 'the new people of God', taught that 'the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from the Holy Scriptures' (Nostra Aetate 4).

Scholars are divided on Hebrews itself. Lloyd Kim (2006) judges it supersessionist 'with qualifications': for him Hebrews holds that Jesus fulfills Israel's priesthood, covenant and sacrifices, but it is an argument among Jews and rejects neither the Jewish people nor their institutions; his reviewer Andrew Massena adds that for modern opponents of supersessionism Hebrews 'offers little guidance'. Jesper Svartvik has traced how 8:13 has been read, from its first setting to its use in modern apologetics. Readers who resist the replacement reading stress that Hebrews argues entirely from Israel's Scriptures, honors Moses and the faithful of Israel (chapter 11), says the new covenant was promised 'with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah' (8:8), and addresses Christians tempted to give up, not Jews outside the church.

Jewish readers answer that the Torah gives Aaron's sons 'a priesthood for all time' (Exodus 40:15), and that Judaism kept faith after the Temple fell, finding atonement in 'the practice of lovingkindness' (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4; see the note on 7:12). This site presents the texts and these readings side by side; see also the notes on 8:13.

Hebrews was copied among Paul's letters from the earliest manuscript we have (P46, about AD 175-225, where it follows Romans), and the Greek-speaking East accepted it early. The West hesitated: Eusebius reports that the church of Rome disputed it, Gaius of Rome counted only thirteen letters of Paul, and the Muratorian fragment does not mention it. Calvin wrote that because the Novatians used 6:4-6 to deny pardon to the fallen, 'those of the Western Church, in particular, refused the authority of this Epistle'. Even late in the 300s Jerome and Augustine record the doubts, but the African councils of the 390s put the letter with Paul's: the Council of Carthage of 397 lists, in its Latin, 'thirteen letters of the apostle Paul, one of the same to the Hebrews' (Pauli apostoli epistolae tredecim, eiusdem ad Hebraeos una). Luther set Hebrews with James, Jude and Revelation at the end of his New Testament, calling it the work of a disciple of the apostles. All churches today hold it as Scripture.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a sermon that hides its preacher
spec.body: Hebrews, like 1 John, never names its writer, and the omission may be deliberate. The whole sermon ranks every human messenger below the Son: the prophets spoke 'in many pieces' (1:1), Moses was an attendant (3:5), Aaron's priesthood passed away (7:23), and the readers' own leaders are honored only as 'the ones who told you the word of God' (13:7). Hebrews also introduces Scripture as God, the Son or the Holy Spirit speaking, and seldom names the human writer it is quoting: once it says God spoke 'in David' (4:7), and it quotes Moses' own words only where Moses is a person in the story (9:20; 12:21). A preacher who argues that God's last word is the Son may have chosen to keep his own name out of the way. The idea that the silence was deliberate is old: Clement of Alexandria thought Paul left his name off so as not to put off Hebrew readers suspicious of him, and an older teacher he calls 'the blessed presbyter' said Paul did it out of respect for the Lord, who was the apostle sent to the Hebrews (Eusebius, Church History 6.14.3-4; compare 3:1). Claude's suggestion differs in tying the silence to the sermon's own argument. It rests on 1:1-2; 2:6; 3:5; 3:7; 4:7; 13:7 and 13:22.

prompts: The high priest behind the veil

A tall woven curtain drawn like a scroll across the page, its edges fading into soft parchment; through a gap, a figure in a plain white linen robe walks into a glow of light, carrying a small bowl; on the near side, a crowd of ordinary people in first-century clothes, men, women and children, look after him. Mix ancient manuscript ink lines, cave-painting figures and a touch of modern watercolor; warm golds and deep blues; soft, rounded edges, no hard rectangle.

A ship's anchor drawn in brown ink, its rope running upward and disappearing through the folds of a great temple curtain into light, while below a small boat rides a stormy sea sketched in cave-painting strokes. Hand-lettered Greek word ANKYRA faint in the margin. Parchment texture, soft torn edges, no frame.

Two figures meet on a rocky road outside a hill town: a priest-king holding bread and a cup of wine, and a weary bearded traveler with armed men and captured flocks behind him. Above them, faint like a watermark, a crowned figure in light. Ancient manuscript illumination mixed with cave-drawing figures and modern line art, soft edges, earthy colors.
